The only thing that might have tripped us up a bit in such a trivial example is if two of the rats had shared the same weight, as observing ties is certainly a possibility. We’ll wash our hands of the likelihood of that happening, though, by making an assumption that will hold throughout this lesson… and beyond.

Making the assumption, though, that there is a near zero chance of a tie happening allows us to develop the distribution theory of order statistics that holds at least approximately even in the presence of ties. In this lesson, we explored a new idea that might seem a little different at first—what happens when we actually care about the order of our data? Instead of just looking at a bunch of values from a random sample, we asked questions like: what’s the probability the third smallest value is below a certain number? Or what does the distribution of the largest observation look like? These kinds of questions bring us into the world of order statistics.

We learned how to define and identify order statistics, like the smallest, largest, or the r-th smallest value in a sample. Then we got into how to find the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and probability density function (PDF) of a specific order statistic. The cool part is that these functions can be derived using tools we already know—like the binomial distribution and some calculus. You saw how the PDF of an order statistic shifts depending on which rank we’re looking at (e.g., smallest vs. largest), which helps explain patterns in real-world data, like extreme weather events or test scores.
This lesson sets us up to use order statistics in inference problems and real applications—anytime we care not just about the data, but how that data is arranged.
